blog_summary: Adrian Colyer summarizes a paper from Microsoft researchers that presents a roadmap for organizations to transition toward a data-driven culture through continuous experimentation. The authors argue that continuous experimentation (CE) is the next logical step after continuous integration (CI) and continuous deployment (CD), enabling bidirectional feedback between companies and customers. The paper introduces the 'Experimentation Evolution Model,' a maturity framework with crawl, walk, run, and fly phases across technical, organizational, and business dimensions. Colyer highlights the model's practicality, based on Microsoft's internal practices and validated through interviews and historical data. He also emphasizes the foundational prerequisites—statistical knowledge and data access policies—and the need for structured logging and metrics to support experimentation. The blog underscores the financial benefits of scaling experimentation, citing Microsoft's hundreds of millions in additional revenue annually.
paper_title: The evolution of continuous experimentation in software product development
paper_abstract: —Continuous experimentation involves practices for testing new functionality on a small fraction of the user base in production environments. Running multiple experiments in parallel requires handling user assignments (i.e., which users are part of which experiments) carefully as experiments might overlap and influence each other. Furthermore, experiments are prone to change, get canceled, or are adjusted and restarted, and new ones are added regularly. We formulate this as an optimization problem, fostering the parallel execution of experiments and making sure that enough data is collected for every experiment avoiding overlapping experiments. We propose a genetic algorithm that is capable of (re-)scheduling experiments and compare with other search-based approaches (random sampling, local search, and simulated annealing). Our evaluation shows that our genetic implementation outperforms the other approaches by up to 19% regarding the fitness of the solutions identified and up to a factor three in execution time in our evaluation scenarios. I. I NTRODUCTION A high degree of automation (e.g., building, testing, and deploying software artifacts) enables companies, and especially Web-based companies, to release new functionality more frequently and faster. Companies such as Microsoft [1], Facebook [2], Google [3], or Netflix [4] are characterized by having hundreds of deployments a day throughout their software ecosystem. Sophisticated monitoring and telemetry solutions keep track of releases and the captured live production data has become the basis for data-driven decision making [5]. Instead of shipping new features or functionality to all users, continuous experimentation practices such as A/B testing [6] or canary releases [7] enable companies to test new features on a small fraction of the user base first.
